Despite funding from lawmakers for two consecutive years, state health officials say uncertainty over future budgets is preventing the program from moving forward
Tommy Smith, who is 10 and loves Batman, was born with a genetic condition that interferes with his body’s autonomic nervous system, which controls involuntary functions like respiration (photo submitted).
A program designed to train and pay parents, guardians or their designees to provide skilled nursing services to Missourians with medical complexities has stalled for a second year because state officials don’t know if there will be money in next year’s budget to support it.
Missouri lawmakers have approved $11 million in each of the past two state budgets for a program that would pay family members to provide complex medical care at home.
But the program has yet to launch, and state health officials say uncertainty about future funding will likely delay it for another year.
The current state budget includes $3.8 million in state general revenue and $7.2 million in federal matching funds to launch a complex care assistant program, which is designed to ease a shortage of home nurses and provide financial relief for families who step in to provide life-sustaining care. The fiscal year 2026 budget included the same amount of funding.
Proponents of the Medicaid program argue it would compensate families for care they already provide and help keep individuals with medical complexities or disabilities out of institutions. They also contend the state would save money by avoiding preventable hospitalizations.
But as Missouri faces growing pressure on its budget, Lisa Cox, communications director for the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, said the department doesn’t expect the program to launch during the current budget year.
“Regrettably, the uncertainty around sustainable funding for an ongoing project has resulted in an implementation timeline that would make it unlikely that any service would be paid before the next fiscal year, which is beyond the authorization of our current budget,” Cox said in an email to The Independent.
The department’s budget request for fiscal year 2028 includes the same level of funding for the program as the current year.
The program would allow parents, guardians, other family members and people with close relationships to Medicaid recipients to be employed through a private duty nursing agency and provide designated services, such as tube feedings and ostomy care, under the supervision of a registered nurse who would be required to visit in person every 60 days.
Complex care assistants would have to be certified nurse assistants or home health aides and undergo additional competency training, Cox said.
Carol Hudspeth, executive director of the Missouri Alliance for Care at Home, told The Independent her organization is “disappointed” that implementation of the program has stalled.

As of November 18, 2026, the 52-week Treasury bill yielded 4.59%. The 26-week bill yielded 4.46%, the 13-week 4.26%, and the 4-week 4.00%. The longest bill pays the most, and it pays more than some of the best-known dividend stocks. For a saver at or near retirement, the real question is whether a stock’s payout is worth giving up a rate the government promises to pay.
How a Treasury Bill Pays You and When Its Rate Resets
A Treasury bill is a loan to the U.S. government maturing in one year or less. You buy it for less than its face value, and when it matures, the Treasury pays you the full face value. The difference is your interest. Bills have no coupon and send you nothing along the way. According to the IRS, bills generally have a 4-, 8-, 13-, 26-, or 52-week maturity period and are issued at a discount in $100 increments.
The rate is set at auction on the day you buy. Hold the bill to maturity, and its income is fixed. When it matures, you get cash back, and to keep earning you have to roll into a new bill at whatever rate the market sets on that day. The 4.59% figure is really just a snapshot.
It goes only to bills bought at that rate. Someone rolling 4-week bills gets a new rate 13 times a year, and someone rolling 52-week bills gets one once a year. The figure stays locked for neither.
Bills carry three risks that savers often miss:
- Reinvestment risk. If rates fall, every rollover pays less. Income that looked steady can shrink quickly.
- Price risk. You can sell a bill through a broker before it matures, but if rates have risen since you bought it, you may get back less than you paid. Holding to maturity avoids this.
- Inflation risk. The face value is a fixed dollar amount, so rising prices eat into what it buys.
The government’s backing has limits too. The full faith and credit of the United States backs repayment of face value at maturity. The guarantee leaves out the price you’d get selling early, the rate on your next rollover, or what inflation does to your buying power. Bills also pay no monthly income. Getting regular checks in retirement requires staggering several maturities.
Dividend Safety Matters More Than Dividend Size
Each investment has a weakness the other lacks. A dividend can be cut. The board decides on each payment and can lower or suspend it at any time. A Treasury bill’s payout is a legal obligation fixed when you buy. A dividend can grow. A board can raise it year after year. A bill’s income changes only when rates change, and then only when you roll over. That makes dividend safety the starting point for any comparison, ahead of yield.

Is A Fed Hike Still Good News For JPMorgan?
Today’s big story: Could Anthropic Stock Fall 25%?
Most investors expect a Fed rate hike to be good news for big banks like JPMorgan Chase. Higher rates let a bank charge more on its loans. On our data, that still holds for the business. It does not hold for the stock.
The short answer is no. Over 21 Fed hikes since June 2006, a fund of big financial stocks beat the S&P 500 in the next three months only 6 times. JPMorgan beat it after 8 of them. Since the latest hike, JPMorgan has lagged the S&P 500 so far, while that fund has beaten it.
How have bank stocks done since the September hike?
The Fed’s rise in the top of its target range to 4.0% took effect on Sept 17, 2026. It was its first increase since the one that took effect on July 27, 2023. From the close the day before through Wednesday’s close, JPMorgan returned -6.6%, counting dividends. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF, called SPY, returned -2.9%.
Two other big banks did worse. Bank of America returned -15.5% and Citigroup -11.3%. Wells Fargo returned -6.5%, about the same as JPMorgan. Our data shows no single confirmed cause for these drops.
JPMorgan has lost 6.6%, counting dividends, since the Fed hike that many owners expected to help it. If JPMorgan is a big part of your savings, that is a fall you have had to sit through. When the market has fallen, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio has lost about 81 cents for every $1 its benchmark lost, on average. See the HQ record.
Did bank stocks ever rise and fall with rates?
They did, day to day. We measured how closely each stock’s daily move tracked the daily change in the 2-year Treasury yield. That yield follows where traders expect Fed rates to go. The measure is called correlation. A high positive score means the two moved together, and a score near zero means no link.
From 2016 to 2019, the yearly score of the Financial Select Sector SPDR fund (XLF) averaged 0.52. JPMorgan’s averaged 0.51. In 2026 so far, XLF’s score is -0.09 and JPMorgan’s is -0.04. The SPDR S&P Regional Banking ETF (KRE), a fund of smaller banks, is at -0.19.
Put simply, bank stocks no longer rise on days when rate expectations rise. SPY now has a negative score too, at -0.13. We think higher yields are trading as bad news for stocks in general.
The table sets the old link next to this year’s, and next to each fund’s record after hikes.
Source: Trefis analysis of Intrinio daily closes, FRED and Treasury.gov yields. Scores are correlations of daily returns with the daily change in the 2-year yield. Hike and any-day results compare total return over the next three months, from June 2006 on.
Do higher rates still help the banks’ business?
Yes. Net interest income is what a bank earns on loans and bonds, minus what it pays on deposits. JPMorgan’s was $27.0 billion in the three months to September. Illicit Gardens cultivation facility in Kansas City (Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent).
Missouri cannabis regulators are asking prospective marijuana research license applicants what they want to study and what obstacles might stand in their way.
The new rules allowing marijuana research in the state go into effect Nov. 30. Ahead of that date, the Missouri Division of Cannabis Regulation is gathering feedback through an online survey “to better understand the interests, needs, and readiness of prospective applicants.”
The survey asks what kinds of studies applicants are considering, what could prevent them from obtaining or using a license and how prepared they are to begin operating.
The new rules leave the door open for many research possibilities, Amy Moore, the division’s director, said earlier this year.
“We’re all very interested in any research on cannabis and safety or its impact on the human body,” Moore said. “Certainly as a public health agency, we’re interested in health research, but it’s not limited to that. So it’ll be interesting to see what people want to propose once we get this established.”
When voters approved recreational marijuana in 2022, the constitutional amendment allowed the state to establish licenses to “facilitate scientific research or education.” But the state first had to adopt regulations. The division released draft rules last year for informal public feedback.
In May, the division asked for another round of public feedback, and the comments and the state’s responses were published in the Missouri Register in October.
A common theme among the comments was whether the state would allow seeds and clones developed through research to help licensed cultivators improve their products.
The division clarified that research licensees can sell or transfer seeds and clones developed through an approved research study to licensed cultivation facilities. Any such sale or transfer must be part of a study approved by the division.
However, marijuana sold to consumers must be grown in a licensed cultivation facility.
“Marijuana grown under experimental research conditions may pose a public health and safety risk,” the division’s response states. “Allowing the transfer of seeds and clones to cultivation facilities allows cultivation facilities to grow and cultivate marijuana plants as required in rule and in a manner that is required to meet specific testing requirements for consumer safety.”
State cannabis law requires all marijuana products sold in Missouri to originate from marijuana grown and cultivated in a Missouri-licensed facility.

But nearly two months after finishing with silver, the American trio could soon have gold added to their résumés.
On Thursday, November 19, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) announced that Kenya's Veronica Loleo had received a three-year doping ban after testing positive for erythropoietin (EPO), a prohibited substance. The decision officially disqualifies her second-place finish at the September 20 event, where her silver medal helped Kenya secure the women's team title. Countries are ranked by the combined finishing times of their three fastest athletes, and Loleo’s removal means Kenya must now count Lilian Kasait Rengeruk, who finished 34th in 1:10:36, potentially lifting the U.S. to first place in the team standings.

On November 13, 2026, chip stocks sold off and the S&P 500 fell 0.4%, although it still gained about 2.5% on the week, according to Yahoo Finance's market coverage. Wholesale inflation also reached its highest annual rate in nearly four years, and the 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.15% on November 13, 2026. What a Price Target Really Means
A price target is an analyst's estimate of where a stock should trade in about 12 months, built from forecasts for earnings, growth and a reasonable valuation multiple. Upside is simply the gap between today's share price and the average of those targets, expressed as a percentage. Because targets are opinions rather than guarantees, they can move quickly after a company reports, and a cut does not always mean the analyst has turned negative. Sometimes a firm trims its target to reflect a stock that has already risen, or an expectations bar that was set too high, while keeping a positive rating.
That is why the rating and the target are best read together. An upgrade with a lower target tells a different story from a reiterated rating with a higher one. The reasons behind a change, such as delayed contracts, better cost control or a pricing shift, usually say more than the number does. Ranking by average upside adds a second layer. When a fund has an uncertain lifespan
Alternative investment funds often have a fixed lifespan. They spend the first few years buying illiquid assets and then spend the remaining years selling them off.
However, fund liabilities can have a long, uncertain lifespan, making their wind-down difficult and slow. Contingent tax liabilities can have a long tail of six or more years due to statutes of limitations in certain US jurisdictions.
Hedge funds can often give investors their money back regularly because they hold assets that are easy to sell based on investor demand for capital. But private equity funds, credit funds, infrastructure funds and real estate funds generally consist of illiquid assets that need to be sold opportunistically and generally can’t provide investors with full liquidity.
As a result, private equity fund managers will frequently advertise an expected investment period and expected fund lifespan – without making any assurances. But investors can be reluctant to invest without an indication of when they’ll see a return on their money.
Fund managers earn performance bonuses (carried interest) based on how quickly they return cash to investors. To hit these targets and wrap up an aging fund, managers sometimes sell their remaining assets to a new, secondary fund, often called a continuation fund backed by a different group of investors or a subset of the original investors.
However, fund managers struggle to control how long a fund’s financial obligations last, and buyers who take over existing funds usually don’t want to inherit old debts and risks. In the investment world, tax liabilities are especially problematic because they can linger for a very long time.
Tax liabilities, a long-tail risk
Certain tax liabilities can, of course, be eliminated by paying the appropriate tax authority. But contingent tax risks relating to uncertain positions taken by the fund can have a significantly longer tail.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration unveiled a final rule on Thursday that will make it easier for companies in some industries to classify workers as independent contractors rather than their employees, who have more legal protections and can cost more.
The Department of Labor scrapped a rule adopted during the administration of former President Joe Biden, and replaced it with a legal test favored by business groups.
The new rule could lower costs for companies in a range of industries, including trucking, healthcare, retail sales and app-based transportation and delivery services such as Uber, that rely heavily on contractors. Such companies routinely face lawsuits accusing them of misclassifying workers to save money, which they deny.
The Labor Department said the 2024 rule was legally flawed and that the new test creates a clearer standard for businesses and workers to follow.
“It’s more important than ever to ensure our labor regulations keep pace with the changing ways that Americans choose to work, and businesses choose to operate,” Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said in a statement.
The rule will take effect in January, 60 days after it is formally published.
New Rule Focuses on Control
The Biden-era rule had established factors for determining whether a worker should be classified as an employee or contractor under federal wage law, and any one of them could tip the scales toward employee status.
The rule finalized on Thursday instead focuses on whether workers are under a company’s control or have the opportunity for profit or loss based on their own initiative or investment.
Employees can cost businesses up to 30% more, according to several surveys, because they are entitled to the minimum wage, overtime pay, unemployment insurance, reimbursements for expenses and other protections not afforded to contractors.
Worker classification has been one of the most contentious employment-related issues over the last decade, and trade groups lobbied heavily to repeal the 2024 rule after an effort by Republicans in Congress to block it stalled.
The Biden-era rule had replaced a regulation adopted during Trump’s first term that said workers who own their own businesses or can work for competing companies — such as a driver who works for Uber and Lyft — can be treated as contractors. The new rule is similar to that standard.

Top officials in Florida this week approved some significant changes to the Florida Hurricane Catastrophe Fund’s reimbursement contract, potentially allowing property insurers to recover much more in living expenses when homeowners are displaced after a storm.

US District Judge Steven Merryday in Tampa, Florida, on Thursday denied a request by one of the world’s most prominent news organizations to dismiss the case, which the president filed last year. Trump accused the news outlet of tarnishing his reputation with false stories about his business acumen before the 2024 presidential election.
The judge dismissed two claims in the suit and narrowed four others. The surviving claims relate to statements accusing Trump of tax fraud, tax evasion, money laundering or related criminal conduct.
Merryday, appointed by former President George H.W. Bush, ruled Trump sufficiently alleged that the Times had acted with “actual malice,” meaning its journalists knew the statements were false or acted with “reckless disregard for the truth.” The actual malice standard — a high bar that must be met by public figures who sue for defamation — was established by the Supreme Court decades ago to protect press freedoms.
However, Thursday’s ruling significantly narrows the case by eliminating more than two dozen challenged statements, mostly from Times articles.
The ruling does not find that the New York Times defamed Trump, but it holds that the allegations are sufficient to survive the newspaper’s motion to dismiss. The decision means the case is now on track for a potential trial.
Merryday held that the disputed Times statements accuse the president of tax crimes without an “explicit opinion from a qualified source after a thorough examination of pertinent facts.”
“Knowing of the necessity for that opinion but failing to procure that opinion is a fine example of the purposeful avoidance of the truth,” the judge said.
The New York Times did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment. A representative of Trump’s legal team also did not immediately respond.
The lawsuit is one of several filed by Trump against the media since the start of his second term. A $10 billion defamation suit Trump filed against the Wall Street Journal was thrown out by a different judge in a ruling that barred him from refiling it. The British Broadcasting Corp. lost its move to dismiss a $10 billion suit brought by Trump.

Can a software comeback and an ordinary valuation bring the stock back near its old peak?
By Daniel Sparks –
Key Points
- IBM's software revenue climbed 9% at constant currency in the third quarter, after 5% growth in the second.
- IBM's adjusted earnings per share rose about 10% in the first three quarters of 2026.
- At the end of 2025, IBM stock traded at about 26 times that year's adjusted earnings.
My best estimate for International Business Machines (IBM -2.04%) is a share price of about $300 when 2030 ends. From roughly $227 as I write, that comes to a rise of about 32%, or about 7% a year before dividends.
I get there by multiplying the non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share I think IBM can earn in 2030, about $16.75, by 18 -- a price-to-earnings ratio in line with the stock's own history.
Even $300 is below the June 2 record close of $329.23. Shares today trade around 31% under that high, and they're down about 23% in 2026.
Image source: Getty Images.
Software carries IBM's profits
Most of this estimate depends on IBM's software business. For the third quarter, the segment made up around 46% of IBM's $17.1 billion in revenue but about 65% of its segment profit (the profit IBM reports for each business line).
Showing how much the business has bounced back, software revenue grew 9% year over year in constant currency (a measure that removes exchange-rate moves) in the third quarter. This was a big acceleration from 5% in the second quarter. And the second quarter had itself marked a slowdown from 8% in the first quarter and 11% in the fourth quarter of 2025. Better yet, software's segment profit margin improved to 35% from 33% a year before, so the segment is keeping more profit per dollar of sales.
In January, management expected software to grow around 10% this year. On IBM's Oct. 21 earnings call, CFO Jim Kavanaugh said the company now sees around 7% to 8%, with 7% as the base case.
But IBM's annual recurring revenue, a yearly run rate for its recurring software business, rose 8% to $24.9 billion in the third quarter. And Kavanaugh said he expects the growth rate to approach double digits in the fourth quarter.
How much can IBM earn by 2030?
IBM's adjusted earnings per share reached $11.59 in 2025, up 12% from 2024. So far in 2026, through September, they've risen around 10% to $7.79. Quarterly growth moved from 19% to 5% to 11% -- the same drop and rebound software went through.

The American Property Casualty Insurance Association is one of eight organizations pushing federal lawmakers to rethink and fine tune legislation regarding consumer choice when it comes to vehicle repair.
The matter, they said, is important because current limitations on just how and where vehicles are fixed has increased the cost of repairs because parts in some cases are limited to more expensive original equipment manufacturer (OEM) options, and access to vehicle-generated diagnostics, data, and software is restricted – especially when it comes to modern vehicles.
A federal standard is needed to ensure consumers have the right to choose who repairs their vehicles and what parts are used.
“According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, over the last five years in the absence of a federal right to repair, vehicle repair costs increased over 40%,” said the groups signing the letter to House Speaker Mike Johnson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. Along with the APCIA, others include the Auto Care Association, CAR Coalition, MEMA Aftermarket Suppliers, Commercial Vehicle Solutions Network, National Federation of Independent Business, National Independent Automobile Dealers Association, and Preventative Automotive Maintenance Association.
They said they’d like to see more provisions within the Right to Equitable and Professional Auto Industry Repair (REPAIR) Act (HR 1566) included in any legislation. Provisions of the REPAIR Act were included earlier this year within another piece of legislation, the Motor Vehicle Modernization Act of 2026 (HR 7389), passed by a House committee. However, REPAIR Act sponsor Neal Dunn (R-Fla.) has said the legislation passed “does not fully reflect the original REPAIR Act and fails to protect consumers, independent repair shops, and aftermarket manufacturers.”
The organizations signing the letter to House leaders apparently agree. The MVMA Act included “repair provisions based largely on limited voluntary memoranda of understanding developed more than a decade ago. These agreements fail to meet automotive repair marketplace needs in 2026,” they said.
“Recent developments underscore why voluntary industry policies are not enough,” the groups continued, adding that General Motors recently released its position that it “strictly prohibits” use of non-OEM parts for repair.
“This guidance effectively restricts consumer choice and forces the use of more expensive OEM parts,” the groups said. “GM’s position statement is illustrative of a broader trend: Several other automakers, including Ford, Honda, and Nissan, have rolled out similar restrictions.
“Consumers should continue to have a choice of lawful, safe, and equivalent repair options.”

Roberta Groner had what she calls “a rocky road” for the year leading up to the New York City Marathon on November 1.
In her previous three attempts at the marathon, during which she had hoped to run an Olympic Marathon Trials qualifying time (2:37), she had racked up three DNFs in a row.
She was in great shape for the Valencia Marathon in December 2025, having just run 1:12:21 for the half marathon, and she thought she might be in shape to better her lifetime PR in the marathon, which is 2:29:09, from 2019, when she was 41. Her conservative goal was getting the Trials time.
But a warm day in Spain—about 75 degrees—and a brain lock about translating kilometers into miles caused her to step off the course late in the race. Her coach, Devon Martin, of the Central Park Track Club, still rues that one. “She had no idea she had seven minutes to spare at mile 18,” Martin said.
Two weeks later, Groner hopped in the Marathon Project in Arizona. Martin had tried to convince her not to. Sure enough, her legs hadn’t recovered from the hard miles in Valencia, and she dropped out there, too.
Then came Grandma’s Marathon in June in Duluth, Minnesota. Groner felt off. She later realized that her body was adjusting to starting hormone replacement therapy for perimenopause symptoms. Another DNF.
By the time she got to New York City, her hometown race, Groner—a former nurse who is now a full-time coach with Central Park Track Club—was uncharacteristically a basket case.
“I had to fight some mental demons, especially the week before,” she said. “My coach was probably like, ‘Oh, I can't handle her.’”
Groner ran with the elite women, always a small group in New York, which leaves those who can’t keep pace with the strange sensation of running a big-city marathon alone. She was well behind the leaders, running side-by-side with Steph Bruce for the first 17 miles, before Bruce fell back. Groner spent the next 9 miles with her eyes scanning the distance for any women she could pick off on the way to the finish.
She passed a handful of runners in the final stretch and finished 22nd in 2:35:55, her third Olympic Trials qualifier. She’ll be 50 when the race goes off in St. Louis. Dot McMahan of Michigan, who has qualified for her sixth trials, will be 51.
“I was able to race and compete, which was great,” Groner said. “And yeah, it wasn't my fastest New York, but I was really happy with the performance. Knowing that my faster days could be done, I still want to race really well. To be able to pass a few people at the end. I’ll give it an A.”
But are her fastest days really behind her? Groner doesn’t necessarily think so. And she’s not backing off her goals just because she’s in her late 40s.

Cindy O'Laughlin, pictured speaking to reporters in May 2024, will lead Missouri's education department as interim commissioner beginning Dec. 1 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Senate President Pro Tem Cindy O’Laughlin, a Shelbina Republican, will lead Missouri’s Department of Elementary and Secondary Education as interim commissioner of education beginning Dec. 1.
The State Board of Education voted 6-1 to appoint O’Laughlin in a closed meeting Friday morning. It will continue its search for a permanent commissioner, aiming to hire a permanent commissioner by June.
“I recognize that this is an interim role, and my responsibility is to provide steady leadership while the board continues its search for a permanent commissioner,” O’Laughlin told The Independent Friday afternoon. “I have told the board I will not be vying for that position. But that doesn’t mean we should stand still.”
The board has “important work underway to improve accountability, establish clear goals and focus on student achievement,” she said. The department is currently working on an A-F grading system for public schools requested by Gov. Mike Kehoe, drawing criticism from educators who fear schools’ reputation will be impacted by a scoring system they see as flawed.
“I am ready to roll up my sleeves and get to work,” O’Laughlin said. “Our kids deserve nothing less.”
She will replace Lisa Sireno, who has served as interim commissioner since Oct. 21 following the resignation of Stacey Preis.
Missouri state education board selects interim commissioner amid leadership shakeup
The announcement came after months of rumors that O’Laughlin was being eyed for the position. As word circulated more widely in the past month, the state board’s inbox filled with angry emails and questions about her qualifications.
Wheaton school Superintendent Alyssa Kennedy was among those who opposed O’Laughlin’s possible appointment, sharing her letter to the board in a Facebook post.
“I respectfully urge the Board not to make this appointment based on political alignment or a predetermined outcome,” she wrote. “If the Board is considering Senator O’Laughlin, I urge you to carefully examine whether her experience and policy positions align with the responsibilities and public mission of this office.”
State law requires the commissioner to “possess an educational attainment and breadth of experience in the administration of public education.”
O’Laughlin’s Senate biography says she has experience “as a school bus driver, an administrator at a local Christian school and as a member of her local school board.” The Independent could not find record of her work in these positions.

In the document, she cites work in the legislature as a key part of her achievements in education.

The 62-33 vote sends the legislation to the U.S. House, where the measure is up against a slim number of days left in the lame-duck session and a host of competing legislative priorities.
The bill would shorten environmental review times and narrow the criteria for triggering the comprehensive reviews required under the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA.
The measure gained approval of most Senate Republicans, who generally support streamlining environmental reviews, and several Democrats who want to see shorter review times for renewable-energy projects.
Opponents voiced concern that NEPA, a bedrock federal statute for environmental protection, would be too severely weakened and that tribes would lose power over the consultation process.
Just two Republicans — Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley and South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds — voted against the bill. On the flip side, only 15 members of the Democratic caucus voted in favor.
The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee’s leaders — GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Democratic Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island — along with the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Chair, GOP Sen. Mike Lee of Utah and ranking Democrat, Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, negotiated the measure.
In a statement celebrating the bill’s passage, Capito said the upper chamber “took a major step towards addressing the affordability concerns of the American people.”
Capito said she has “spent years trying to achieve bipartisan compromise on legislation that gets our nation back to building,” adding that the bill “is the culmination of those efforts.”
In his own statement, Heinrich said the measure would bring down electricity costs while preserving environmental standards.

President Donald Trump has backed the measure, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA. In a statement of administration policy this month, the administration said the bill would “deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and economic growth across the United States.”
